police-room-calendar.title: Find the meeting room calendar
police-room-calendar.description: Help staff find the weekly room calendar that’s already in their booking tool.

goal: When someone asks for a meeting room, I open the booking calendar and click through each room to see when it’s free. Then I tell the person which room is available. It takes too many clicks.
process: I look at each room one at a time until I find an open slot, then tell the person which room to book.
existing: A coworker showed me the weekly view. It already shows which rooms are free side by side.
barrier: Most of us don’t know where to find the weekly view. A quick show-and-tell would help.
data: We just need room names and free or busy times.
systems: This is all in the booking calendar we already use.
changes: We only need to look at the calendar.
impact: If I read it wrong, I can check the room’s calendar again.
owner: The front desk lead is responsible for room bookings. Our team is already allowed to see the weekly view.
boundary: These are ordinary office meeting rooms.

fire-renewal-view.title: See staff renewals due soon
fire-renewal-view.description: Show upcoming staff renewal dates in the team’s current workbook, with an IT review of who can see the information.

goal: Each Monday I check our staff training workbook for renewals due in the next 30 days. I read each row and mark what’s coming up for the training coordinator. I’d like a saved view that shows the rows I need to check.
process: I open the workbook, compare each renewal date to the calendar, and tell the training coordinator which items are due soon.
existing: We have the workbook, but there isn’t a saved view for renewals coming up.
data: The workbook contains staff names and individual training renewal dates. This is private staff information.
systems: The view would stay in our current workbook in the same restricted folder.
changes: It would only show matching rows. It would never change dates or send anything.
impact: I’d compare the view with the workbook before doing anything with the list.
owner: The training coordinator and HR own the workbook. They’ve allowed our training office to use it for renewal reminders. IT should check who would be able to see the new view.
boundary: This is for office reminders. We aren’t using it to assign shifts or decide whether someone can work.
frequency: I do this each Monday. It takes about 15 minutes.
rules: Show any renewals coming due in the next 30 days.
input: Every row has the same columns, including the renewal date.
output: A view in the same workbook that shows only renewals due in the next 30 days.
exceptions: If a renewal date is blank, the coordinator checks the original record by hand.
people: Only the training office staff who already use the workbook.
tools: We already use the approved workbook in a restricted folder. We’d use that same file.
review: The training coordinator would compare the view against the original dates before using it.

comms-practice-kit-notes.title: Sort practice kit notes and update the log
comms-practice-kit-notes.description: Have AI suggest a category for practice-kit notes, then use a rule to update the matching row after staff approve.

goal: After a training session, I read the notes people leave about the practice kits. I decide whether each note is about sound, the screen, or a missing part, then find that kit in our log and type the category. I’d like help with those two steps.
process: I start with a note and a kit number. I read what happened, pick a category, and write that category on the row for the same kit number.
existing: We checked the note form and the kit log. Neither can read the notes and fill in the category.
data: It’s just practice kit numbers and notes about the parts. No staff details or call records.
systems: After I approve the draft, I’d like the note form to pass the category to the practice kit log. IT would need to check whether those two tools can talk to each other.
changes: After I approve a category, the log would fill in the category on the matching kit row.
impact: A wrong entry could send us looking for the wrong part. We can correct it in the training log.
owner: The training lead owns both lists and has agreed to look at this with IT.
boundary: This is only for practice kits kept in the training room. None of them are used to take calls.
frequency: It happens after training sessions. I see about ten notes a week.
rules: Someone has to understand the note. Finding the kit’s row is always an exact match on kit number.
input: A form with a kit number and a box where people describe the problem in their own words.
judgment: I can read the original note and see whether the suggested category makes sense.
output: Give me a suggested category and the note to check. Once I approve it, put the category on the row for that kit.
exceptions: If there’s no kit number or more than one row matches, leave the log alone and let me handle it.
example: If kit P-04 has a note that says ‘voices were hard to hear,’ suggest Sound. After I approve it, put Sound on the P-04 row.
people: The training room team uses the log.
tools: The form and log are available, but we don’t know what approved tool can help read the notes or pass the category along.
review: The training room coordinator reads the original note, checks the kit number, and approves or corrects the category before the log changes.

fire-office-supply-list.title: Make the Friday office supply list
fire-office-supply-list.description: Use the same reorder rule each Friday to make a list of office supplies to buy.

goal: Each Friday I count printer paper, pens and folders and enter the numbers on our inventory form. I copy the low items onto a list for the office lead. I’d like the list made for me.
process: I look at the current count and the reorder number for each item, write down the ones that are low, then hand the list to the office lead.
existing: The form stores the counts. We checked with the office lead and it can’t make the low-stock list.
data: Office supply names, counts and reorder numbers.
systems: A person can download the counts as a file. The list can be made from that file.
changes: Make the list for me to check. I’ll give it to the office lead myself.
impact: I can compare it to the counts and fix it before I use it.
owner: The office lead owns the supply list and has agreed we can test this.
frequency: Every Friday. There are about 20 items, and making the list takes about 10 minutes.
rules: Put an item on the list when its count is at or below its reorder number.
input: A file with the same three columns every week: item, count and reorder number.
output: A list of item names with counts at or below the reorder number.
people: Just the office lead and me.
tools: We don’t have an approved tool that will apply the rule to the file and make the list for us.

police-training-forms.title: Find the right training forms
police-training-forms.description: One place to find training forms, with open questions about which forms and who keeps them current.

goal: Could we have one place to find the right training forms? I keep asking around because I can’t tell which copy is the latest.
process: When I need a form, I look in a shared folder or ask a coworker. Different people send me different copies.
existing: Someone mentioned there might already be a page for this. I haven’t seen it.
data: I’m not sure if we’d point to blank forms or if people would expect to see their completed forms too.
systems: I know there’s a shared folder. I don’t know where the other copies live.
changes: I don’t know whether we need a list of links or somewhere to upload forms.
impact: It’s frustrating using the wrong form, but I don’t know what else it could affect.
owner: I don’t know who keeps the forms current.
boundary: I’m asking about finding office training forms. This isn’t about emergencies or decisions on behalf of the public.
frequency: I ask when I need a form. I don’t know how often other people do.
rules: We don’t have an agreed way to tell which version to use.
review: I don’t know who should make sure a form is current.

comms-display-guide.title: Draft a training room display guide
comms-display-guide.description: Turn trainers’ rough notes into a one-page display guide that a staff member checks before sharing.

goal: When the training room setup changes, I collect trainers’ written tips about connecting a laptop and choosing the display input. I compare the tips with the room setup, write a one-page guide, and share the checked version with our trainers. It takes about 45 minutes when the steps are scattered across several notes. I’d like an AI tool to draft the guide from notes we give it, with a source note for each step. It should flag disagreements and leave out details it can’t verify. Our training lead would check the draft against the notes and try the steps in the room before sharing. This is for the classroom display only.
process: When we replace an adapter or move the display, trainers send me short notes about what worked. I read the notes, try the steps in the training room, and ask a trainer if anything is unclear. I write the steps in order and give the guide to our training lead. Once they’ve tried the steps and signed off, I put the guide in the training folder.
existing: We checked our training folder and the room’s setup sheet. The template gives us a place to write the guide, and the setup sheet explains the hardware. Neither combines the trainers’ notes or tells us where their instructions disagree.
data: Use only classroom setup notes: cable types, display menu labels, and the order people tried the steps. For a test I’d write sample notes from scratch. Leave out names, logins, network details, staff records, and anything from a live call or dispatch system.
systems: I would paste the sample notes into a drafting tool that IT approves for the test, then copy the checked text into our guide template by hand. There’s no connection to the display, to any file store, or to a system that handles calls.
changes: The tool only reads the notes we give it and returns text. It has no write access to our training folder, cannot change display settings, and doesn’t send or publish anything. Staff would decide what to keep and where to put it.
impact: If the draft names the wrong display input, the trainer catches it during a room check and fixes it before sharing. We can set the draft aside and keep using the checked instructions already in the room.
owner: The training lead owns the guide and the setup notes. They’ve approved trying the idea with made-up notes and want IT to confirm what tool we can use. The lead still signs off on any version people will use.
boundary: This guide is for a standard classroom screen used for staff training. It does not affect live dispatch, emergency response, or access to any operational system.
frequency: I revise the guide when the equipment or setup changes, around six to eight times a year. Writing and checking the first version takes about 45 minutes. For a trial I’d time the whole job, including reading the sources and trying the steps, to see if the draft saves at least 15 minutes.
rules: It requires interpretation because three trainers can mean the same thing by ‘switch the screen over,’ ‘select the laptop input,’ and ‘pick HDMI.’ The guide needs to combine those notes and keep their meaning. The layout can stay the same, but a checklist or keyword rule alone can’t tell which instruction is supported.
input: The inputs are short notes written in people’s own words, sometimes as a list and sometimes as a paragraph. I can label them Note A, Note B, and so on, but the wording and order vary. We’d give the tool only the handful of notes for one room setup.
output: I want a one-page draft with a ‘Before you start’ list, numbered setup steps, and a ‘Needs a check’ box. Each step should point back to the note it came from. The draft should leave a disputed detail out of the steps and put both versions in the check box. Staff make any updates to the guide by hand.
judgment: I can compare every suggested step against the source notes and try it on the display. For the trial we’d use ten made-up note sets with expected steps and include examples that disagree. A draft passes only if every step has a source, the order works when we try it, and every disagreement is visible.
exceptions: If notes conflict, show both and flag the point for a trainer to check in the room. If there’s a missing step or a note is too vague, mark it as missing rather than filling it in. For example, if one note says to pick HDMI 1 and another note says HDMI 2, flag both input names for a room check before including an input in the guide.
example: Note A says ‘Connect the HDMI cable before turning on the screen.’ Note B says ‘Use HDMI 2,’ and Note C says ‘Use HDMI 1.’ The draft should include the cable step with Note A as its source. It should flag the two input names and leave the input number out until we test it in the room.
people: The training resources coordinator prepares the draft. The training lead reviews it and runs the steps in the room. The small group of trainers uses the checked one-page guide.
tools: We have the shared guide template and the original setup notes. We haven’t picked an approved AI drafting tool for this use. I’d ask IT about a local or City-approved option that can work from only the notes we supply.
review: The training lead checks each line against its source note, resolves anything flagged, and tries the steps on the actual classroom display before sharing. They can edit or discard the draft. If it adds unsupported instructions or misses a disagreement, we use the manual process and record what failed.

fire-badge-access.title: Check badge requests for the records room
fire-badge-access.description: Flag missing or mismatched information before staff approve badge access to the personnel records room.

goal: I help process badge requests for the Fire personnel records room. When a supervisor sends a request, I check whether the employee is active, whether their job is on the approved access list, and whether temporary access has an end date. Then the records manager approves the request and Building Security updates the badge. I spend time chasing missing dates. I’d like the form to flag missing or mismatched details before approval. The records manager would still approve each request, and Building Security would make the badge change. A wrong change could let someone see confidential staff files.
process: I start with a supervisor’s request. I compare it with the staff roster and approved job list, then mark any missing details. I give the checked request to the records manager. If they approve it, Building Security changes the badge.
existing: Our badge system can apply an approved change. We checked with Building Security and it doesn’t run these three checks on incoming requests.
data: The checks use private staff information, including employment status, job role, and who has asked for access. We can test with made-up requests and a made-up roster.
systems: I’d like the request form to check an approved copy of the staff roster and job list. Ask IT whether those sources can share just the fields the form needs. The form leaves the badge system alone.
changes: The form only reads the fields it needs and shows what is missing or doesn’t match. The records manager approves each request. Building Security makes any changes to badges.
impact: If a wrongly cleared request led to a bad badge change, someone could enter the locked room and see confidential staff files.
owner: The records manager owns the room access list, HR owns the staff roster, and Building Security manages badges. They’ve agreed to use made-up requests for a review. IT still needs to confirm which roster fields can be used and where.
boundary: The form supports an office approval process. It flags details for staff to check. The records manager decides who may enter the room, and Building Security applies that decision.
frequency: I do this whenever a supervisor sends a request. Most weeks there are a few. A request with missing details can take a second round of emails.
rules: Flag the request if the roster doesn’t show the person as active, the job doesn’t match the approved list, or a temporary request has no end date.
input: A request form with the same fields each time, an approved job list, and a staff roster with employment status.
output: A short checklist showing which fields matched and which ones staff need to check before the request goes for approval.
exceptions: If a request has a missing date or the job doesn’t match, I ask the supervisor to check it. If the roster is unavailable, I pause the request and check with HR. For example, if a temporary access form is missing its end date, flag the missing date and leave the badge unchanged.
example: A supervisor requests two weeks of temporary access but leaves the end date blank. The checklist should flag the blank date. I ask for the date and keep the request pending.
people: Fire office staff check requests, the records manager approves them, and Building Security makes badge changes.
tools: We have an approved badge system for applying changes. We haven’t found an approved tool for doing these request checks.
review: The records manager checks the request against the approved list and signs off before Building Security changes a badge. Staff return an incomplete request and can check the information by hand.
